meta.blurb: Meet Maya, who wants to turn an idea for fixing bicycles at people's doors into a hundred paying customers. Step by step, she learns to test her guesses cheaply, listen to real people and count what matters.
meta.bible: Maya: a keen bicycle mender with an idea for a business that repairs bicycles at office workers' workplaces; she is the running example. Dev: one of the first cyclists she interviews, who tells a story about a broken chain. Rosa: Maya's first paying customer, who later returns with a friend. Ken: a customer who complains that Maya arrived late. Ayla: a friend who is good with computers and offers to build a booking tool. Northgate: the area of offices where Maya starts. Riverside Cyclists: a local cycling group where she posts her offer. All people, places and numbers in the story are made up as examples. The book's own ideas: a business idea is a bundle of guesses; talk to ten real people and ask about the past; praise is not a customer; name a price early; offer the smallest version by hand; ask for a real commitment; keep a notebook; count real actions; follow a chain of steps and fix the weakest step; change one thing at a time; set a target and a time limit and decide beforehand what would make you continue, change or stop; know what it costs to win and serve a customer; repeat customers show real value; change the customer or the problem, not just a detail, if nothing works. Voice and tone: practical, kind and encouraging, one clear idea or step in each beat; no invented statistics, studies or real companies.

beats.scene: Maya sits at her kitchen table with a bicycle wheel and a notebook
beats.summary: Maya has an idea for a business that repairs bicycles at people's doors, and she wants her first hundred customers.

beats.scene: Four sticky notes on a wall, each with one short question
beats.summary: Her idea feels finished, but it is really a bundle of four guesses: people have the problem, will pay, are enough, and can be reached.

beats.scene: Maya's garage is full of unused tools and a half-built cart
beats.summary: If she builds everything first, she may spend months before learning that one guess was wrong.

beats.scene: Maya crosses out the words perfect plan and writes learn fast
beats.summary: In the early days the aim is to learn quickly, not to be perfect.

beats.scene: Stepping stones lead across a shining stream towards the far bank
beats.summary: A hundred customers is a path of small steps: first one, then ten, then thirty.

beats.scene: A cyclist in a work jacket locks a bike at a rack at dawn
beats.summary: Start with one kind of person, not with the product: Maya chooses office workers who cycle to work.

beats.scene: Maya counts bicycles at the racks in a small office car park
beats.summary: A narrow group is easier to find: Maya picks the offices of Northgate.

beats.scene: Maya pins a card with one written sentence above her desk
beats.summary: Write the problem as one sentence, in the customers' own words.

beats.scene: A cyclist pushes a flat-tyred bike along a pavement, looking tired
beats.summary: A real problem leaves traces: people have tried to fix it, spend time or money on it, or complain about it.

beats.scene: Maya talks with a cyclist beside a bike rack, notebook in hand
beats.summary: Before building anything, hold about ten conversations with people who might be customers.

beats.scene: A cyclist points at a worn bike chain while Maya listens
beats.summary: Ask about what people did last time, not about what they might do in future.

beats.scene: A smiling cyclist gives a thumbs-up while keeping a hand on his wallet
beats.summary: People are polite, and praise such as great idea does not mean they will pay.

beats.scene: Dev tells Maya a story, waving his hands, while she writes
beats.summary: Listen for stories, details and feelings, and write down the exact words.

beats.scene: Maya spreads ten pages of notes across the floor and draws lines
beats.summary: After ten talks, look for what several people said, not what one person said.

beats.scene: Maya reads her notes beside a clock showing the end of the workday
beats.summary: People do not mind paying for repairs; what they hate is losing time, because the shops close when they finish work.

beats.scene: Maya crosses out a sentence on a card and writes a new one
beats.summary: Change the guess, not the dream: she will now repair bikes at the office while owners work.

beats.scene: Maya writes a clear offer, with price and time, on a small card
beats.summary: Describe your offer in one clear sentence: what you do, for whom, and when.

beats.scene: A price written on a card is held up beside a bicycle wheel
beats.summary: Name a price early, because a price shows whether people really want it.

beats.scene: Maya packs a small bag of tools and a paper notebook
beats.summary: Offer the smallest version that can help one real person, and do the work by hand first.

beats.scene: Maya types a short message on her phone beside a printed note
beats.summary: Make it easy to say yes: a short message and a one-page note with a clear way to book.

beats.scene: A cyclist hands Maya a small deposit while she writes a name
beats.summary: Ask for a real commitment, such as a booking or small deposit; actions are stronger than words.

beats.scene: Maya pins a note on a noticeboard beside the bike racks
beats.summary: Find your first customers where they already are: friends, local groups and noticeboards.

beats.scene: Rosa smiles and points down the street as Maya takes notes
beats.summary: Ask each person who else has the same problem; one conversation leads to the next.

beats.scene: Maya records a friendly voice message on her phone for a customer
beats.summary: At the start, do personal things that a big company never could.

beats.scene: Maya hands a hand-written card to a customer with an honest smile
beats.summary: Be honest that the service is new; never pretend to be bigger than you are.

beats.scene: Maya tightens a bolt on Rosa's bicycle while Rosa watches
beats.summary: Rosa becomes her first paying customer, and Maya does her best work and watches Rosa's reactions.

beats.scene: Rosa and Maya talk beside the finished bicycle in the sun
beats.summary: After the job, ask: what almost stopped you from booking? How would you describe this to a friend?

beats.scene: A notebook with dates and neat notes lies open beside a coffee cup
beats.summary: Keep a simple notebook: date, who, what you tried, what happened, what you learned.

beats.scene: Maya draws tally marks on a whiteboard under four headings
beats.summary: Count real actions, such as bookings, not likes or views.

beats.scene: Four boxes on a whiteboard are linked by arrows, with numbers inside
beats.summary: Follow the steps people take: how many see it, reply, book and come back.

beats.scene: Maya circles one small number on the whiteboard in red
beats.summary: Find the step where most people drop out and fix that first.

beats.scene: Maya holds two versions of her note side by side
beats.summary: Change one thing at a time so you can tell what made the difference.

beats.scene: A calendar with Friday circled and a number written beside it
beats.summary: Set a time limit and a target before each test: by Friday, three of ten will book.

beats.scene: Maya writes three words on a card: continue, change and stop
beats.summary: Decide beforehand what result would make you continue, change, or stop.

beats.scene: A crumpled note lies in a bin beside a notebook with a new line
beats.summary: A test that fails is still a result, and because the test was small, the cost is small.

beats.scene: Maya hands out printed notes beside the bike racks at Northgate
beats.summary: Choose one way of reaching customers and work at it until you understand it.

beats.scene: Maya counts printed notes in a pile beside a small stack of coins
beats.summary: Work out what it costs to win one customer: add up money and time, then divide by the bookings.

beats.scene: Rosa returns with her bicycle and a friend beside her
beats.summary: Do customers come back? If they do not, the problem may not be solved well enough.

beats.scene: Maya asks a customer a question while handing back the bike
beats.summary: Ask how people would feel if you stopped; if many would be very disappointed, you have something valuable.

beats.scene: A customer hands a small card with Maya's number to a colleague
beats.summary: Word of mouth grows when it is easy to share: give customers a card and a reason to pass it on.

beats.scene: Two price cards, one lower and one higher, held up beside a bicycle
beats.summary: Many beginners charge too little: test a higher price with new customers.

beats.scene: Maya writes numbers in two columns labelled money in and money out
beats.summary: Know what it costs to serve one customer and to win one; you must earn more than both.

beats.scene: Maya writes a checklist on a card for a repair visit
beats.summary: Write down the steps so that you can repeat them, teach them, and spot what wastes time.

beats.scene: Maya hands her checklist to a friend who wants to help
beats.summary: Get help or software only after you have done the task many times and know what is needed.

beats.scene: Ken frowns beside his bicycle while Maya listens carefully
beats.summary: A complaint is a free lesson: reply quickly and fix the cause.

beats.scene: Maya's calendar is full of bookings with gaps kept for checks and rest
beats.summary: As customers grow, protect the quality and add one new thing at a time.

beats.scene: A hand-drawn map with two arrows leading from one bike rack to different offices
beats.summary: If many honest tests show nobody wants it, change the customer or the problem, and keep what you learned.

beats.scene: Maya crosses off the last square on a wall chart of one hundred squares
beats.summary: Maya reaches her hundredth customer, a stranger who heard about her through a friend's card.

beats.scene: Maya writes a letter to herself at the kitchen table, notebook beside her
beats.summary: Looking back, Maya sums up the steps: choose a person, listen, test small, ask for commitment, count honestly.

beats.scene: A line of bicycles stands at the racks in the morning light
beats.summary: Takeaway: guess, test small, listen, count honestly, change early, and repeat; your first hundred customers are a hundred lessons.

B1B2: Maya loves bicycles, and she has an idea for a business. She wants to fix people's bikes at their front doors, and she hopes to find a hundred customers.
To Maya, the idea feels like a complete business that only needs a little time. In truth it is a bundle of four guesses, and her first job is to find out which of them are true.
Maya could spend months buying tools and making a website. If one guess is wrong, she would only find out after the money and time are gone.
In the early weeks, the goal is not to be perfect. The goal is to learn as much as possible, as cheaply and as quickly as possible.
A hundred customers sounds like a mountain. But Maya sees it as stepping stones, with the first customer, then the first ten, then thirty, and onward.
Maya does not start by describing her service. She starts by choosing one kind of person, the office workers who cycle to work, and she thinks about their mornings.
Maya picks the offices in one area called Northgate. A small and clear group is easier to find and to talk to than a whole city.
Maya writes the problem in one sentence, in words that a customer might use. It says that the bike needs mending, and the shop is only open when people are at work.
How can Maya tell if the problem is real? There are three signs: people have already tried to solve it, they spend time or money on it, and they complain about it.
Maya makes a firm promise to herself before she spends any money at all. She will have ten real conversations with people who cycle to work before she buys tools or builds a website.
Maya learns to ask about the past. She asks when the bike last broke, and what happened next, instead of asking whether someone would use her service.
Maya notices that people are polite. They say it is a great idea, but a compliment costs nothing, and it is not the same thing as a customer.
Dev tells her a long story about his broken chain and a ruined morning. Maya writes down his exact words, because the small details are the most useful part.
After ten conversations, Maya lays out her notes and looks for patterns. One strong opinion is only a story, but the same complaint from several people is a signal.
Maya's notes show a surprise. Most people do not mind paying for repairs, but they hate losing time, because the bike shops close at the hour when they finish work.
Maya decides to change her plan, and she does not feel bad about it. She will fix bikes in the office car park while the owners are busy at their desks.
Maya writes a clear offer on a small card. It says what she will do, for whom, and when, so that anyone can understand it in a few seconds.
Maya adds a price to her offer. A price is a test of its own, because people only take an idea seriously when they know what it will cost.
Maya asks what the smallest version of her service could be. She needs only a bag of tools, a paper notebook and a free hour, and she does every step by hand.
Maya writes a short message and a one-page note about her offer. The note ends with a very clear and easy way to say yes.
Maya learns to ask for something real, such as a booking for a certain day. Actions like this are much stronger signs than words, because they cost the person something.
Maya looks for her first ten customers in places where cyclists already gather. She posts in the Riverside Cyclists group and puts a note beside the bike racks.
After each conversation, Maya asks whom else the person knows who has the same problem. One kind introduction can easily lead to three more.
Maya writes to each person by name and remembers what they told her. A large company could not afford such care, but at the start it is her greatest advantage.
Maya is honest with everyone she meets. She tells them that her service is new, that she is just beginning, and that she values their advice.
Rosa becomes the first paying customer, and Maya does her best work. She also watches carefully how Rosa responds, since every reaction is a lesson.
When the job is done, Maya asks Rosa two questions. What almost stopped you from booking, and how would you describe this service to a friend?
Maya keeps a simple notebook with five columns: the date, the person, what she tried, what happened, and what she learned. She reads it every Friday.
Maya counts the numbers that matter. She counts how many people book, not how many people look at her posts or press the like button.
Maya draws a short chain of steps on her whiteboard to follow each person. Out of every ten people who see her note, how many reply, how many book, and how many come back?
Looking at her chain, Maya sees that many people reply but few of them book. This is the weakest step, so that is where she decides to work first.
Maya is tempted to change her price, her note and her times all at once. Instead she changes only the booking step, so that she can tell what made the difference.
Before every test, Maya writes down a target and a time limit. For example, by Friday, three out of ten people should book a repair.
Maya also decides, before a test begins, what result would make her continue, change her plan, or stop. This protects her from fooling herself after the numbers arrive.
One of Maya's tests fails, because nobody wants to book a repair on a Sunday. Instead of feeling beaten, she writes down the lesson, and she is glad that the test was cheap.
Maya could try posters, adverts, emails and social media all at once. Instead she picks one way of reaching customers and works at it until she understands it.
Maya adds up the cost of her printed notes and her time, and she divides by the number of people who booked. This shows her what it costs to win one customer.
Maya watches to see who comes back for a second visit. When customers return, the problem is really being solved, but when they do not, she needs to find out why.
Maya asks her regular customers how they would feel if she stopped coming. If many say that they would be very disappointed, she knows that she has found something valuable.
Happy customers want to tell others, but they need a simple way to do it. Maya gives each of them a small card, and a good reason to pass it on.
Many beginners charge too little because they are afraid. Maya offers a slightly higher price to her next new customers, and almost nobody minds.
Maya now writes down what it costs to serve a customer, from tools and travel to her own time. Each customer must bring in more than this cost, and more than the cost of finding them.
After doing the job many times, Maya writes the steps on a checklist. A written process is easier to repeat, to teach to someone else, and to improve.
Ayla, a friend who is good with computers, offers to build a simple booking tool. Maya says yes, because she has done every step by hand and knows exactly what the tool must do.
Ken complains because Maya arrived thirty minutes late for his repair. She apologises at once, and then she changes her booking messages so that no one is kept waiting without warning.
With more customers, Maya is busy, and it is easy to hurry. She protects her quality by adding only one new thing at a time and by checking that each customer is still happy.

Imagine that Maya had tried many honest tests and still nobody wanted her service. She would not give up on learning, but she might change the customer or the problem, and keep everything she had learned.
After many months, Maya reaches her hundredth customer, a stranger who heard about her from a friend. She crosses the last square off her chart and sits quietly for a minute.
Maya looks back and writes down what she would tell herself at the start. Choose a real person, listen to them, test small, ask for a commitment, and count honestly.
The path to your first hundred customers is much the same for any business. Make a guess, test it in a small way, listen carefully, count honestly, and change early.
C1C2: Maya has spent years mending bicycles as a hobby, and now she has an idea for a business that would bring those skills to people's front doors. She does not yet have a customer, a price, or even a name, but she has a goal of one hundred paying customers. This book follows her, one small step at a time, and shows how anyone can do the same.

To Maya the business already feels finished, with its tools, its customers and its happy cyclists, but in truth it is a bundle of four guesses. People have a problem worth solving, they would pay for a solution, there are enough of them to make a living from, and she can reach them without spending a fortune. She writes each guess on a sticky note, and the wall suddenly looks far less certain, and far more honest.

Maya could easily spend six months buying equipment, designing a logo and building a website, all before she speaks to a single customer. If even one of her guesses is wrong, she would discover it only after the money and the months were gone. Learning early, while the cost is small, is the only safe way to begin.

Maya decides that for the first few weeks her goal will not be perfection, since perfection is a luxury for people who already know what customers want. Her goal will be to learn as much as she can, as cheaply and as quickly as she can, about the people she hopes to serve. Every conversation and every small test will be a step towards knowing.

A hundred customers sounds like a mountain to someone who has none, but Maya decides to think of it as a river crossed on stepping stones. First she needs one customer, then ten, then thirty, and each stone teaches her how to find the next. By the time she reaches the far bank, she will have learned things that no plan made at a desk could have told her.

Instead of beginning with a description of her service, Maya begins by choosing one kind of person, the office workers who cycle to work in her town. She pictures their mornings, their locked bikes and their small frustrations, and she asks herself what a day looks like from their side. The service can be shaped later, but the person has to be real from the start.

A whole city is far too large a target, so Maya picks one place, the offices of Northgate, where a few hundred people work within a short walk of one another. A group that is small and clearly defined is much easier to find, to talk with and to serve than a crowd of strangers. She can reach several of them this very week.

Maya now writes down the problem she thinks she can solve, in a single sentence and in the words a customer would use, not in the words of a business plan. Hers says that the bike needs mending, and that the shop is only open when the owner is at work. If she cannot put the problem simply, she suspects that she does not yet understand it.

Before going any further, Maya wants to know whether the problem is truly painful or only mildly annoying. A real problem leaves traces, and she looks for three: people have already tried to solve it, they are spending time or money on it today, and they complain about it to anyone who will listen. Where none of these signs exist, she knows that she should be careful.

Maya makes herself a firm promise that she will hold ten real conversations before she spends a single coin on tools, signs or websites. Each one will be with a person who cycles to work in Northgate, and none of them will be a friend who simply wants to be kind. Ten is not a scientific number, but it is enough to show her whether she is on the right road.

Maya soon learns that the best question is not whether someone would use her service, because people are poor at predicting their own behaviour. Instead she asks about the past, for example when the bike last broke and what happened next, since a real event tells her much more than an opinion. What people have done is a better guide than what they say they will do.

Maya notices that almost everyone she meets is kind, and many of them tell her that the idea is wonderful. A compliment, however, costs the speaker nothing, and it is not the same thing as a customer who is ready to pay. She learns to listen for what people do, what they have spent and what they have tried, and to treat praise with friendly caution.

Dev, one of the first cyclists she speaks to, tells her a long and rather angry story about a broken chain that left him pushing his bike through the rain on the morning of an important meeting. Maya writes down his exact words, because she knows that the details of such stories are far more useful than any summary. Stories show what people care about, how they behave, and what they have already tried to do.

When the tenth conversation is finished, Maya spreads her notes across the floor and begins to look for patterns. One strong opinion is only a story, she reminds herself, but the same complaint repeated by several people is a signal worth following. She circles every sentence that appears more than twice and leaves the rest for later.

The notes contain a surprise, for most of the cyclists do not mind paying for repairs, and several admit that they have no wish to learn how to do them. What they dislike is the loss of time, since the nearest shops close at about the hour when they leave work. The real problem is not broken bikes but a lack of convenient hours.

Maya adjusts her idea, so that she will now repair bicycles in the office car park while their owners sit at their desks. At first she wonders whether changing the plan means she was wrong, but she soon sees that it means she has learned something real. A guess that has been corrected is worth more than a guess that was never tested.

Now that her idea has changed, Maya writes a clear offer on a small card, stating what she will do, for whom, and when she will do it. She tests it by reading it aloud to a friend, who must be able to repeat it back after a few seconds. An offer that cannot be explained quickly will not be bought quickly either.

Maya adds a price to her offer, although she is a little afraid that it will frighten people away. She learns that a price is itself a kind of test, because people treat an idea very differently once they are asked to hand over money for it. A customer who hesitates at the price teaches her as much as one who agrees.

Maya asks herself what the smallest version of her service might be that could still help a real person, and the answer surprises her by being so small. She needs no van, no website and no app, only a bag of tools, a paper notebook and a free hour, and she will handle every step by hand. Doing the work herself will teach her what matters, so that anything she builds later will be built for a reason.

Instead of a complicated website, Maya writes a short message and a one-page note describing her offer, and she ends it with a simple way to book a time. A reader should be able to understand it in less than a minute and to say yes with a single reply. If she has to explain it again and again in person, she will know where it needs to be clearer.

Maya learns to ask for something real, such as a booking for a definite time or a small deposit, rather than for opinions. A commitment costs the person something, even if only a little time or money, and so it tells her far more than a polite remark. The bigger the step a person takes, she realises, the more their answer is worth.

For her first ten customers, Maya does not wait for people to find her, but goes to the places where cyclists already gather. She posts her offer in the Riverside Cyclists group, pins a note beside the bike racks at Northgate, and tells every person she has already talked to. The first customers are often the people who are closest to us, and there is no shame in beginning there.

At the end of every conversation, Maya asks the same polite question, which is whether the person knows anyone else who has the same problem. A recommendation from a friend carries a trust that no advertisement can buy, and one kind introduction often leads to three more. She thanks each person warmly, and she remembers who helped her.

At the start, Maya does many things that a large company would never do, such as writing to each person by name, remembering what they told her, and calling to confirm a booking. These small acts take time, and they could not be repeated for ten thousand customers. For a hundred, however, they are not only possible but valuable, because they teach her what people truly value.

Maya is tempted, once or twice, to make her business sound bigger and older than it really is, but she decides against it. She tells people openly that the service is new, that she is still learning, and that their advice will help her improve it. Most people, she finds, are happy to help someone who is honest, and many enjoy being part of a beginning.

Rosa becomes Maya's first paying customer, booking a repair for a bicycle with a loose brake and a squeaking chain. Maya does the best work she possibly can, and she also watches Rosa's face, her questions and her pauses, because each reaction is a small lesson. Her goal is not just a satisfied customer but a clearer picture of what the service is really worth.

When the job is finished, Maya asks Rosa two questions that she will ask every customer from now on. What almost stopped you from booking, and how would you describe this service to a friend? The answers show her the doubts that other people may be feeling, and the words that others might use when they speak about her.

Maya keeps a simple notebook with five columns, which record the date, the person she spoke to, what she tried, what happened, and what she learned. Each Friday she reads through the week's entries and looks for the lessons that she would otherwise forget. Memory, she has discovered, tends to flatter us, whereas a page of notes tells the truth.

Maya decides to count only the numbers that tell her something real, which means the people who book and pay and not the people who look and smile. A post with a hundred likes and no bookings, she realises, has taught her only that the post was pleasant. Numbers that make her feel good are not always the numbers that help her to grow.

On her whiteboard Maya draws a short chain of steps, from seeing her note to replying, booking, paying and finally coming back for a second visit. She writes a number under each step for every week, so that she can see exactly where people stop. A chain like this turns a vague feeling of how things are going into a picture that she can read.

Looking at her chain, Maya sees that many people reply with interest but only a few go on to book a time. This is the weakest link, and she knows that improving anything before it would be like pouring water into a leaking bucket. She decides to find out why people hesitate, and to repair that step before doing anything else.

Maya is tempted to change her price, her wording and her available times all in the same week, hoping that something will work. She resists, because if several things change together she will never know which of them made the difference. A single change, followed by a careful look at the results, teaches her far more than a dozen at once.

Before each test begins, Maya writes down a target and a deadline, such as three bookings out of ten messages by the end of Friday. The target gives her something to aim at, and the deadline stops a test from drifting on for months while nobody looks at the result. Without these two things, she realises, it is far too easy to see success in anything.

Maya also decides in advance what result would make her carry on, what would make her change her approach, and what would make her stop altogether. Choosing the rules before the numbers arrive protects her from the very human habit of explaining away whatever disappoints her. It is much easier to be honest with oneself when the question has been asked first.

One of Maya's tests fails completely, for nobody at all wants to book a repair on a Sunday morning. Instead of feeling beaten, she writes down the lesson in her notebook and is grateful that the test took only an hour and cost nothing. A failed test that was small and quick, she sees, is not a disaster but a bargain.

Maya could try posters, newspaper adverts, emails, social media and a dozen other things at the same time, but she knows that her time is limited. She chooses one way of reaching customers, handing out notes beside the bike racks, and keeps at it until she understands how well it works. Once one method is reliable, she can add a second without losing track of either.

Maya adds up the cost of the notes she printed and the hours she spent handing them out, and she divides the total by the number of people who booked. The result is what it costs her to win one customer, and it surprises her, because her own time is the largest part. A business that spends more on winning a customer than that customer will ever bring in will eventually run out of money.

By the second month, Maya is more interested in who comes back than in who comes once. A customer who returns without being asked is telling her, in the most honest way possible, that the problem was really solved. When people do not return, she knows that something is wrong, and she goes to ask them why.

Near the end of each month, Maya asks her regular customers a simple question, which is how they would feel if she stopped coming. Some shrug, but several say that they would be very disappointed, and one says that she would have to start taking the bike to a shop again. Those who would truly miss the service, Maya understands, are the people for whom she is solving a real problem.

Satisfied customers often wish to tell their friends, but they rarely do so unless it is easy and gives them a reason. Maya therefore hands each customer a small card with her name and number, and offers a free chain clean to anyone who brings a friend. Within three weeks, a good share of her new bookings come from those cards.

Many beginners charge too little because they fear that nobody will pay more, and Maya is no exception. With her next group of new customers, she tries a price that is a little higher than before, and she watches carefully to see whether the number of bookings falls. Almost nobody objects, and she realises that her old price had been a guess that was too cautious.

Maya now works out what it costs her to serve one customer, counting parts, travel and her own hours, and she adds this to the cost of finding that customer in the first place. Only if a customer pays more than the two costs together will the business grow stronger with every sale. Doing this arithmetic early, before she is busy, helps her to avoid the painful surprises that come with success.

After dozens of visits, Maya knows the job so well that she can finally write down every step, from the greeting to the final test ride. A written process is easier to repeat, to teach to another person, and to improve, and it shows her which steps still waste her time. She would not have been able to write it well in the first week, when she did not yet know what mattered.

Ayla, a friend who is good with computers, offers to build a booking system for Maya, and for the first time the offer makes sense. Maya has done every step by hand for weeks, and she knows exactly which steps are slow, which are important and which can be thrown away. Help that comes after understanding is far more useful than help that comes before it.

Ken complains, quite fairly, because Maya arrived half an hour late for his repair and gave him no warning. She does not make excuses but apologises at once, repairs the bike without charge, and changes her booking process so that every customer receives a message if she is delayed. A complaint, she has come to believe, is a free lesson from someone who cared enough to say what went wrong.

As the bookings grow, Maya finds herself hurrying, and she notices that the quality of her work is beginning to slip. She decides to protect it by adding only one new thing at a time, by leaving a little time between visits, and by checking that every customer is still pleased. Growth that damages the thing customers loved in the first place is not progress but a slow way of losing them.

Suppose that after many honest and well-designed tests, Maya had found that almost nobody wanted her service. Giving up would be one choice, but a better one might be to change something large, such as the kind of customer or the exact problem she tries to solve, while keeping everything she has learned. A change of direction made with evidence in hand is not a failure but a more intelligent next step.

On a cool morning many months later, Maya crosses the last square off her chart, because her hundredth customer is a stranger who heard about her through a friend's card. She remembers how far away that number seemed when she first wrote it down at her kitchen table, and how much she has learned on the way. The business is no longer a bundle of guesses, but a collection of things she has proved, one customer at a time.

Looking back, Maya writes a short note to the person she was on the first day, listing what she wishes she had known. Choose a real person, listen to the stories they tell, test your ideas in the smallest way possible, ask for a real commitment, and count the numbers that matter. The list is short, she notices, and almost all of it was within her reach from the very beginning.

Whatever your business may be, the path to your first hundred customers follows the same simple rhythm of making a guess, testing it in the smallest way you can, listening with care, and counting honestly. When the result is not what you hoped, change something early, while the cost is still small, and then begin the cycle again. Your first hundred customers, in the end, are a hundred lessons, and the best day to begin collecting them is this week.
